questions.title: Does a statutory mandate for a government agency to act create a 'concrete injury' for the party who requested the action?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the court's reasoning regarding the 'procedural right in vacuo.' The opinion mentions that Section 1216(a)(3) says OSC 'shall' conduct an investigation, but the court says this isn't enough for Article III standing. If a statute explicitly mandates that an agency perform a specific task upon a request, why isn't the failure to perform that task considered a concrete injury to the person who made the request?

questions.title: How does the 'speculative chain' analysis affect redressability in cases involving multiple agencies?
questions.question_body: In this case, the court rejected AFL's theory that forcing OSC to investigate would eventually lead to DOJ releasing records. The court describes a chain: OSC $\rightarrow$ MSPB $\rightarrow$ DOJ. I understand that courts don't like speculation, but if the whole point of the statutory scheme is to provide a mechanism for correction, at what point does a 'causal chain' become 'too speculative' to satisfy the redressability requirement of Article III?

questions.title: What is the distinction between a statutory duty to investigate and a statutory right to receive information?
questions.question_body: AFL argued they had an informational injury because they weren't getting the 'fruits' of the OSC investigation. The court seems to distinguish between OSC's duty to investigate under Section 1216 and AFL's right to actually receive information under Section 1214. I'm confused: if the investigation is mandatory, doesn't the result of that investigation naturally belong to the party that triggered it, or is 'informational standing' only possible if the statute explicitly says 'the agency shall provide the results to the requester'?

questions.title: Can a court find that an agency committed a 'legal error' but still refuse to order a remedy based on 'discretion'?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the district court's ruling mentioned in the opinion. The district court found that OSC made a 'legal error' by refusing to investigate, but then declined to order them to do so because the decision was 'committed to OSC's discretion.' This seems contradictory—how can a decision be both a 'legal error' and 'discretionary' at the same time? Does this relate to the concept of agency deference or the 'committed to agency discretion' review standard?

questions.title: What is the functional difference between OSC investigations under 5 U.S.C. § 1216 and 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses two different ways OSC can get involved in FOIA withholdings: one under section 1216(a)(3) and one under section 552. The OSC argued they couldn't investigate because the triggers for section 552 weren't met. I don't understand if these are two separate 'paths' to the same result, or if section 552 acts as a limitation on the power granted by section 1216. Which one takes precedence when a party asks for an investigation?
